alex-g>elliott-smith.found: Giannascoli admits that some of these analogs work, especially Modest Mouse and Smith. “I’ve been really influenced by Elliott Smith’s singing style,” he says.
alex-g>elliott-smith.citation: Alex G to Consequence (Geoff Nelson, "Ruining Alex G", 2015): "I've been really influenced by Elliott Smith's singing style... When you sing like that, in a kind of whispery way... I do it for no other reason than it makes it easier to sing in tune, to hit all the notes correctly. And also I didn't want to wake my roommates and shit, because a lot of times I was recording at night."
alex-g>elliott-smith.note: The old citation clipped the roommates sentence mid-way. I dropped the OndaRock quote because I did not locate or verify it.

arca>aphex-twin.found: I think his musical tastes left a big influence on me. He had a lot of Aphex Twin, Squarepusher.
arca>aphex-twin.citation: Arca to GRAMMY.com (Jennifer Velez, 2021), on her older brother's records: "I think his musical tastes left a big influence on me. He had a lot of Aphex Twin, Squarepusher." The FADER's "Cover Story: Arca Finds Xen" (Emilie Friedlander, 2014) also describes her teenage Nuuro songs as "glitchy, Aphex Twin-inspired beat compositions."
arca>aphex-twin.note: Both pages were opened and read. The FADER line is in the journalist's voice. The GRAMMY quote supplies the first-person tier.

arca>squarepusher.found: I think his musical tastes left a big influence on me. He had a lot of Aphex Twin, Squarepusher.
arca>squarepusher.citation: Arca to GRAMMY.com (Jennifer Velez, 2021): "I have a brother seven years older, and I would often borrow his music... I think his musical tastes left a big influence on me. He had a lot of Aphex Twin, Squarepusher."
arca>squarepusher.note: This is Wikipedia footnote [8], followed to the source. The old citation skipped the sentence that actually states the influence.

arca>autechre.found: Aided partly by his older brother’s CD collection, he went through a series of musical obsessions typical of kids growing up in the ’90s—Aaliyah, Autechre, Nine Inch Nails, Marilyn Manson—and started spending more and more time on the internet.
arca>autechre.citation: The FADER (Emilie Friedlander, "Cover Story: Arca Finds Xen", 2014) reports that, aided partly by an older brother's CD collection, Arca went through "a series of musical obsessions typical of kids growing up in the '90s—Aaliyah, Autechre, Nine Inch Nails, Marilyn Manson."
arca>autechre.note: This is the journalist's narration, not Arca's words, so I changed the tier from first-person to reported. The 2014 article uses pre-transition pronouns.

depeche-mode>gary-numan.found: It’s funny, but I really liked the early Gary Numan records, yet never really saw that as something I could do myself.
depeche-mode>gary-numan.note: Vince Clarke (founding member, left after Speak & Spell) told MusicRadar (Danny Turner, 2023) that he liked early Numan but never saw it as something he could do himself. He says OMD and the Human League are what made him think he could. That is fandom, but he places the formative push elsewhere, and he is one departed member. Options: keep as first-person with the citation rewritten to Clarke's own words, or remove. The current citation quotes a Wikipedia sentence that does not exist and is not first-person in any case.

geese>interpol.note: The old citation ("Rolling Stone feature") was unlocatable, so I replaced it with this Still Listening interview.

mogwai>fugazi.note: Ran two new searches for Braithwaite on Fugazi, Ian MacKaye, Repeater and Steady Diet. Neither turned up a Mogwai member on Fugazi. I opened Westword's Braithwaite 'musical roots' Q&A (https://www.westword.com/?p=40647786): it names the Velvet Underground, the Cure, the Jesus and Mary Chain, Bauhaus, Ultra Vivid Scene and Mudhoney, but not Fugazi. The only Fugazi link remains Wikipedia's Rough Guide line, which is not first-person. Proposal: remove, or keep as reported only if the Rough Guide text itself can be checked.

my-bloody-valentine>the-jesus-and-mary-c.found: We don’t have a shared influence… this kind of Cocteau Twins, Jesus and Mary Chain thing, it’s garbage. You know, Psycho Candy would be the shared record.
my-bloody-valentine>the-jesus-and-mary-c.note: The source is Mixdown (Isabella Venutti, 2024). Shields calls the shared Cocteau/JAMC influence idea "garbage" and concedes Psycho Candy "would be the shared record." He then says "everything The Jesus and Mary Chain did back then we were not doing." Later in the same interview he lists JAMC's first single, alongside Einstürzende Neubauten's live show, among things "pulling towards" MBV's early direction. Mixed evidence. Options: keep as first-person with a citation naming Mixdown 2024 and quoting both sides, or record as a partial denial. The current citation names no source. I opened the Westword Q&A lead: it has no JAMC statement.

nick-cave-and-the-bad-seeds>david-bowie.found: “David Bowie’s not merely a performer,” he noted, “He was part of our childhood. In my eyes, Bowie stands for a certain kind of immortality”.
nick-cave-and-the-bad-seeds>david-bowie.citation: Far Out Magazine, relaying Nick Cave's 2013 interview with the German magazine Spex, quotes him: "David Bowie's not merely a performer... He was part of our childhood. In my eyes, Bowie stands for a certain kind of immortality," and calls Cave "a massive admirer of David Bowie and his artistry."
nick-cave-and-the-bad-seeds>david-bowie.note: One search did not find the Spex original. Far Out relays Cave's words secondhand, so the tier is reported. The old citation's specifics ("idol", owning all the early albums and the Berlin trilogy) appear nowhere I could verify, so I dropped them.

siouxsie-and-the-banshees>david-bowie.found: It was no coincidence that so many people involved in punk at the beginning had been inspired by him. Bowie was the catalyst who'd brought a lot of us, the so-called Bromley Contingent, together.
siouxsie-and-the-banshees>david-bowie.citation: Siouxsie Sioux, foreword to MOJO's David Bowie special edition (dated November 2003): "I was 15 when I first saw David Bowie... I just couldn't believe how striking he was... It was no coincidence that so many people involved in punk at the beginning had been inspired by him. Bowie was the catalyst who'd brought a lot of us, the so-called Bromley Contingent, together. And out of that really small group of people, a lot happened including Siouxsie And The Banshees."
siouxsie-and-the-banshees>david-bowie.note: This page is a fan-site transcription of her own signed MOJO foreword, and it is the original of the 'couldn't believe how striking he was' quote. The NPR and AllMusic items in the old citation were not located, so I dropped them.

sonic-youth>black-flag.found: In an interview two years ago, Thurston stated that his intention in starting Sonic Youth was to combine the bone-splitting intensity of Throbbing Gristle (Britain’s seminal and monolithic un-punk squall masters) and the reckless energy of Black Flag (America’s dukes of the hard-noise arena).
sonic-youth>black-flag.citation: SPIN (August 1985 issue) reports that Thurston Moore had said in an earlier interview that "his intention in starting Sonic Youth was to combine the bone-splitting intensity of Throbbing Gristle... and the reckless energy of Black Flag." Moore also includes Black Flag's Damaged in NYLON's "Thurston Moore On 9 Albums That Shaped His Life and Music" (2014), calling Black Flag "the most physical, engaged band I had ever witnessed."
sonic-youth>black-flag.note: This replaces the pipeline-worded Ranaldo/SST citation. The SPIN line paraphrases Moore, so the tier is reported. I opened NYLON (https://www.nylon.com/articles/thurston-moore-9-albums-shaped-life-music); it adds first-person fandom from the early '80s.

xiu-xiu>joy-division.found: The oft-asked question “are they kidding?” is best answered by the sticker affixed to Knife Play, which serves as both a thank you to sources of inspiration and a frank warning shot to would-be listeners: “When my mom died I listened to Henry Cowell, Joy Division, Detroit techno, the Smiths, Takemitsu, Sabbath, Gamelan, ‘Black Angels’ and Cecil Taylor (Jamie Stewart).”
xiu-xiu>joy-division.citation: Trouser Press (Leon Avelino) describes the sticker on Xiu Xiu's debut Knife Play as "a thank you to sources of inspiration": "When my mom died I listened to Henry Cowell, Joy Division, Detroit techno, the Smiths, Takemitsu, Sabbath, Gamelan, 'Black Angels' and Cecil Taylor (Jamie Stewart)."
xiu-xiu>joy-division.note: The sticker itself is only a 'what I listened to' list. Reading it as inspiration is Trouser Press's interpretation, so the tier is reported. Xiu Xiu also covered Joy Division's "Ceremony" on Chapel of the Chimes; a cover does not count as influence.

arcade-fire>neutral-milk-hotel.found: I thought that Magnetic Fields and Neutral Milk were about as good as anything. I didn’t know any better songwriters than those guys.
arcade-fire>neutral-milk-hotel.citation: Win Butler, Red Bull Music Academy lecture (Montréal, 2016): "They had In the Aeroplane Over the Sea by Neutral Milk Hotel, which is just a complete classic... I thought that Magnetic Fields and Neutral Milk were about as good as anything. I didn't know any better songwriters than those guys. My dream was to be on Merge, basically."
arcade-fire>neutral-milk-hotel.note: I read the full transcript; the lecture text matches the old citation. I dropped the rs500albums claim because I did not verify it. Butler speaks of admiring Neutral Milk Hotel as songwriters while founding the band, but the passage also concerns label choice. Owner may want to judge whether that is enough for influence.
